overview: Unit 3 introduces proof by contradiction (Widerspruchsbeweis) through the pigeonhole principle (Schubfachprinzip) and the irrationality of $\sqrt2$ (Irrationalität von √2). Contraposition (Kontraposition) and counterexamples (Gegenbeispiele) show how implications can be proved or refuted; the unit also explains the labels used for mathematical statements (Bezeichnungen mathematischer Aussagen). It then covers sets, listing (Auflistung) their elements, von Neumann numerals (Von-Neumann-Zahlen), selection and separation (Auswahl und Aussonderung), and replacement (Ersetzung). Russell's paradox (Russellsche Antinomie) shows why set formation must be restricted to a fixed starting set.

entries.short: A proof by contradiction assumes the negation of a claim and derives a contradiction from it.
entries.explanation: To prove a statement $A$, first assume $\neg A$. From this assumption and the statement's premises, draw consequences until an impossible statement follows. Then $\neg A$ cannot hold, so $A$ holds. The contradiction must actually follow from the contrary assumption and the premises.
entries.example: Suppose that no weekday occurs four times among 22 days. Then there could be at most $7\cdot3=21$ days, contradicting the 22 days under consideration.
pitfalls: A surprising consequence is not necessarily a contradiction.
The contradiction must follow from the contrary assumption and the premises in force.
entries.heading: Widerspruchsbeweis

entries.short: If more objects are distributed than categories can hold at a specified maximum per category, some category must exceed that maximum.
entries.explanation: If $N$ objects are distributed among $k$ categories, at least one category contains at least $\lceil N/k\rceil$ objects. If every category contained at most $r$ objects, there would be at most $kr$ objects altogether. Therefore, $N>kr$ implies that at least one category contains more than $r$ objects.
entries.example: Among 22 days and seven weekdays, some weekday must occur at least four times, because $22>7\cdot3=21$.
pitfalls: The categories must cover every possible assignment of the objects.
To establish a specific frequency bound, account for the numbers of objects and categories.
entries.heading: 22 Tage und 7 Wochentage

entries.short: Among any 22 days, at least four fall on the same weekday.
entries.explanation: The seven weekdays are the categories to which the 22 days are assigned. Under the contrary assumption that no weekday occurs four times, each weekday would occur at most three times. Thus, at most $7\cdot3=21$ days would be possible, even though 22 days are being considered. This contrary assumption leads to a contradiction.
entries.example: The days need not be consecutive; for the proof, only their assignment to one of the seven weekdays matters.
pitfalls: The claim does not require four consecutive days to fall on the same weekday.
The argument depends on the number of weekdays and the number of days, not on specific calendar dates.
entries.heading: 22 Tage und 7 Wochentage

entries.term: Fraction in lowest terms (Vollständig gekürzter Bruch)
entries.short: A fraction $m/n$ is in lowest terms if $n\ne0$ and $\operatorname{ggT}(m,n)=1$.
entries.explanation: Here, $m,n\in\mathbb Z$, and the greatest common divisor is computed using the absolute values of the numerator and denominator. The condition means that the numerator and denominator have no common positive divisor other than 1. Every rational number has a representation as a fraction in lowest terms.
entries.example: $6/8$ is not in lowest terms, whereas $3/4$ is in lowest terms because $\operatorname{ggT}(3,4)=1$.
pitfalls: The denominator must not be zero.
Different fractions can represent the same rational number, even if only one of them is in lowest terms.
related: Without loss of generality (o. B. d. A.)
Rational numbers as pairs (Rationale Zahlen als Zahlenpaare)
entries.heading: Warum $\sqrt2$ nicht rational ist

entries.term: Without loss of generality (o. B. d. A.)
entries.short: Without loss of generality means that a simplifying choice does not restrict the generality of the argument.
entries.explanation: The abbreviation stands for without loss of generality. When proving the irrationality of $\sqrt2$, one may choose a hypothetical rational representation in lowest terms, since every rational number has such a representation. This choice simplifies the proof without ruling out any possible rational representation of the number.
entries.example: The representation $6/8$ can be replaced by $3/4$ without changing the rational value it represents.
pitfalls: A simplifying assumption is valid only if the chosen representation covers every relevant case.
entries.heading: Warum $\sqrt2$ nicht rational ist

entries.short: The number $\sqrt2$ is irrational because a representation as a fraction in lowest terms would make both numerator and denominator even.
entries.explanation: Assume $\sqrt2=m/n$ with $m,n\in\mathbb Z$, $n\ne0$, and $\operatorname{ggT}(m,n)=1$. Squaring gives $m^2=2n^2$, so $m^2$ is even and hence $m=2k$ for some $k\in\mathbb Z$. Substitution gives $n^2=2k^2$, so $n$ is also even. Thus, $m$ and $n$ both have 2 as a divisor, contradicting $\operatorname{ggT}(m,n)=1$.
entries.example: The derivation assumes that the rational representation is in lowest terms; this is possible because every rational number has a representation in lowest terms.
pitfalls: The inference that an integer with an even square is itself even must be justified.
The contradiction arises because both numerator and denominator are even, although their greatest common divisor is supposed to be 1.
related: Even square of an integer (Gerades Quadrat einer ganzen Zahl)
entries.heading: Warum $\sqrt2$ nicht rational ist

entries.short: A counterexample is a single case that refutes a general claim.
entries.explanation: For a claim intended to hold for every object in a domain, a single object for which it is false is enough to refute it. For an implication $P\Rightarrow Q$, the counterexample must satisfy the premise $P$ and violate the conclusion $Q$. An example in which the claim holds does not prove it in general.
entries.example: The claim If $n^2$ is positive, then $n$ is positive is false: for $n=-1$, $n^2=1>0$, but $n<0$.
pitfalls: For an implication, a case with a false premise does not refute the implication.
A counterexample refutes a claim, but it does not prove another general statement.
entries.heading: Nicht jede ähnlich aussehende Folgerung stimmt

entries.short: The implication $P\Rightarrow Q$ is logically equivalent to its contrapositive $\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$.
entries.explanation: To prove $P\Rightarrow Q$, one can therefore assume that $Q$ is false and show that $P$ is then also false. The converse $Q\Rightarrow P$ is not generally equivalent to the original implication. Contraposition and converse must not be confused.
entries.example: To show that for integers, evenness of $n^2$ implies evenness of $n$, prove instead: If $n$ is odd, then $n^2$ is odd.
pitfalls: The converse $Q\Rightarrow P$ is not the contrapositive.
The proof must use the same domain and premises as the original statement.
entries.heading: Nicht jede ähnlich aussehende Folgerung stimmt

entries.short: If the square of an integer is even, then the integer is also even.
entries.explanation: Prove the statement by contraposition. If $n\in\mathbb Z$ is odd, there is a $k\in\mathbb Z$ such that $n=2k+1$. Then $n^2=(2k+1)^2=4k^2+4k+1=2(2k^2+2k)+1$, so $n^2$ is odd. Therefore, an integer with an even square cannot be odd.
entries.example: Since $6^2=36$ is even, 6 itself is even.
pitfalls: The statement concerns integers, for which the terms even and odd are defined.
The proof establishes a general implication, not merely that individual examples satisfy the statement.
entries.heading: Nicht jede ähnlich aussehende Folgerung stimmt

entries.short: The proof strategy depends on the form of the statement and on whether it is to be proved or refuted.
entries.explanation: A proof by contradiction establishes a statement by deriving a contradiction from its negation. An implication can be proved directly or by proving its contrapositive. A general claim can be refuted with a suitable counterexample. These methods serve different purposes and are not interchangeable at will.
entries.example: For an implication $P\Rightarrow Q$, it may be easier to use $\neg Q$ to derive the statement $\neg P$.
pitfalls: A counterexample refutes a claim, but it does not prove another general claim.
The converse of an implication is not a substitute for its contrapositive.
entries.heading: Widerspruchsbeweis

entries.short: Labels such as definition, theorem, lemma, and corollary classify mathematical statements by their function.
entries.explanation: A definition (Def) specifies the meaning of a term. A theorem (Thm) is an important statement, while a lemma (Lem) is an auxiliary result used in a further proof. A corollary (Kor) follows immediately from a theorem, and a proposition is an independently proved statement. The German label Fakt means fact; the notes give Fkt as its abbreviation and observe that it is rather uncommon as a formal heading.
entries.example: A lemma can prove a subclaim that is later used in a theorem.
pitfalls: A definition specifies a meaning; it is not simply a theorem to be proved.
A heading replaces neither the statement itself nor its proof.
entries.heading: Bezeichnungen mathematischer Aussagen

entries.short: A system of linear equations is a collection of linear equations that must be satisfied simultaneously.
entries.explanation: A solution is an assignment of values to the variables that satisfies every equation in the system. In linear equations, variables appear only to the first power and are not multiplied by one another. A system may have no solution, exactly one solution, or multiple solutions.
entries.example: The system $x+y=3$, $x-y=1$ has the solution $x=2$, $y=1$.
pitfalls: A solution must satisfy all equations simultaneously.
An equation such as $xy=1$ is not linear because it contains a product of variables.

entries.short: A set collects distinct objects and is determined by its elements.
entries.explanation: For a set, what matters is whether an object belongs to it. The order and repetition of elements in a listing do not change the set, since $\{1,0\}=\{0,1\}=\{0,0,1\}$. Elements of a set can themselves be sets.
entries.example: $\{\mathbb N,\mathbb N_0\}$ is a set with two elements, each of which is a set of numbers.
pitfalls: A set is not an ordered list.
An element listed more than once still counts only once in the set.
entries.heading: Mengen: Grundidee

entries.short: The statement $x\in M$ means that $x$ is an element of the set $M$.
entries.explanation: The symbol $\in$ is read as is an element of, and $x\notin M$ means is not an element of. For every object $x$ and every set $M$, exactly one of the statements $x\in M$ or $x\notin M$ holds. The membership relation describes belonging, not order or subset inclusion.
entries.example: For $M=\{2,4\}$, $2\in M$ and $3\notin M$.
pitfalls: The membership relation $\in$ is not the same as the subset relation $\subseteq$.
entries.heading: Mengen: Grundidee

entries.short: The empty set $\varnothing$ contains no elements.
entries.explanation: It can be written as $\varnothing$ or as $\{\}$. For every object $x$, $x\notin\varnothing$. The empty set is itself a set and should not be confused with an unknown value.
entries.example: In the shorthand notation used here, $[0]=\mathbb Z_0=\varnothing$.
pitfalls: $\varnothing$ and $\{\varnothing\}$ are different, because the second set contains the empty set as an element.
entries.heading: Mengen: Grundidee

entries.term: Number sets and the axiom of infinity (Zahlenmengen und Unendlichkeitsaxiom)
entries.short: The axiom of infinity guarantees an infinite set as a foundation for constructing the natural numbers and further number systems.
entries.explanation: $\mathbb N_0$ denotes the natural numbers including 0, while the convention for $\mathbb N$ must be specified. The notes also use $\mathbb P$ for the prime numbers, $\mathbb Z$ for the integers, and $\mathbb R$ for the real numbers. From an infinite set, one can construct $\mathbb N_0$; building on it, further number systems such as $\mathbb Z$, $\mathbb Q$, $\mathbb R$, and $\mathbb C$ can be constructed.
entries.example: $-3\in\mathbb Z$, whereas $\sqrt2\in\mathbb R$ and $\sqrt2\notin\mathbb Q$.
pitfalls: Whether $0\in\mathbb N$ holds depends on the convention that has been specified.
Not every real number is rational.
entries.heading: Mengen: Grundidee

entries.short: A listing gives the elements of a set inside curly braces.
entries.explanation: $x\in\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}$ holds exactly when $x$ occurs in the list. Strictly speaking, a listing must be finite and complete. Ellipses are clear when a pattern or an additional description uniquely specifies which elements are meant.
entries.example: $\{0,2,4,6\}$ lists the four even numbers from 0 to 6.
pitfalls: Ellipses without an explanatory pattern can leave unclear which elements are meant.
Order and repetition do not change the set being represented.
entries.heading: Auflistung

entries.short: For $n\in\mathbb N_0$, $[n]$ denotes the numbers from 1 to $n$, and $\mathbb Z_n$ denotes the numbers from 0 to $n-1$.
entries.explanation: The definitions are $[n]:=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ and $\mathbb Z_n:=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$. For $n=0$, both sets are defined to be empty. This notation represents sets by listing their elements.
pitfalls: $[n]$ starts at 1, whereas $\mathbb Z_n$ starts at 0.
In this notation, $\mathbb Z_n$ denotes the listed set, not automatically arithmetic modulo $n$.
entries.heading: Auflistung

entries.short: The symbol $:=$ means is defined as, and $:gdw$ means if and only if in a definition.
entries.explanation: In $A:=B$, the notation on the left is specified by the expression on the right. The symbol $:gdw$ marks a definition by a condition and expresses an equivalence. Both notations make explicit that a meaning is being specified.
entries.example: $[n]:=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$ defines the shorthand $[n]$.
pitfalls: $:=$ marks a definition, not merely an equality between expressions introduced earlier.
$:gdw$ represents equivalence in both directions, not a one-way implication.
entries.heading: Auflistung

entries.short: The von Neumann numeral $\langle n\rangle$ is the set of von Neumann numerals for the smaller natural numbers.
entries.explanation: The construction begins with $\langle0\rangle:=\varnothing$ and sets $\langle n\rangle:=\langle n-1\rangle\cup\{\langle n-1\rangle\}$ for $n\ge1$. Thus, $\langle1\rangle=\{\varnothing\}$ and $\langle2\rangle=\{\varnothing,\{\varnothing\}\}$. For $m<n$, $\langle m\rangle\in\langle n\rangle$.
entries.example: $\langle3\rangle=\{\langle0\rangle,\langle1\rangle,\langle2\rangle\}$.
pitfalls: The natural number $n$ and its set representation $\langle n\rangle$ are distinct objects.
The notes mark the short relation $x\le y$ / $x\in y$ as unclear; for this representation, what is certain is that $m<n$ implies the membership relation $\langle m\rangle\in\langle n\rangle$.
related: Number sets and the axiom of infinity
entries.heading: Von-Neumann-Zahlen

entries.short: Integers and rational numbers can be described using pairs of numbers, with different pairs sometimes representing the same numerical value.
entries.explanation: The product $\mathbb N_0\times\mathbb N_0$ can serve as a starting point for constructing the integers, and fractions can be described using pairs from $\mathbb Z\times(\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\})$. These product sets are not, by themselves, exactly the number systems $\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb Q$. A complete construction must identify pairs representing the same numerical value as equivalent; the notes do not work out these identifications.
entries.example: The pairs $(1,2)$ and $(2,4)$ represent the same fraction, since $1/2=2/4$.
pitfalls: A Cartesian product is not automatically the number system whose elements the pairs represent.
Different pairs can represent the same numerical value.
related: Number sets and the axiom of infinity
entries.heading: Von-Neumann-Zahlen

entries.short: Selection filters a fixed set to retain exactly the elements that satisfy a given property.
entries.explanation: For a set $A$ and a property $P$, $\{y\in A\mid P(y)\}$ is the subset of elements of $A$ for which $P$ holds. We have $x\in\{y\in A\mid P(y)\}\iff x\in A\land P(x)$. The starting set limits which objects can be selected in the first place.
pitfalls: The property alone does not replace a fixed starting set.
The selection or separation meant here is not automatically the axiom of choice.
entries.heading: Auswahl und Ersetzung

entries.short: Replacement collects the uniquely determined function values $f(y)$ for every $y$ in a set $A$.
entries.explanation: Given a fixed set $A$ and a uniquely determined function $f$, the set $\{f(y)\mid y\in A\}$ is formed. An object $x$ belongs to it if and only if there is a $y\in A$ such that $x=f(y)$. Different inputs may yield the same function value; that value is still counted only once in the image set.
pitfalls: Exactly one function value must be determined for each input element.
Replacement collects function values, not the inputs from $A$.
entries.heading: Auswahl und Ersetzung

entries.short: Here, a set formation is well-defined if its starting set is fixed and its membership conditions or function values are uniquely determined.
entries.explanation: For selection, a fixed set $A$ must already be given, and it must be possible to decide uniquely for each element whether it satisfies the condition. For replacement, exactly one function value must also be determined for each input element. This uniquely specifies which objects belong to the resulting set.
entries.example: The selection $\{x\in\mathbb Z\mid x^2=4\}$ is well-defined and yields $\{-2,2\}$.
pitfalls: A function must assign exactly one value to each input element, but different inputs may have the same value.
An arbitrary condition over all objects, without a specified starting set, can lead to contradictions.
entries.heading: Auswahl und Ersetzung

entries.term: Bound variables and conditions in set-builder notation
entries.short: A bound variable may be renamed consistently, and a comma between conditions means AND.
entries.explanation: In $\{x\in A\mid P(x)\}$, $x$ is bound and can be replaced by a fresh name if all its occurrences are renamed consistently. A comma between conditions means that both conditions must hold at the same time. In such set-builder expressions, a colon can be used as a separator, like a vertical bar.
entries.example: $\{x\in A\mid P(x),Q(x)\}=\{x\in A\mid P(x)\land Q(x)\}$ and $\{x\in\mathbb R:|x|<1\}=\{y\in\mathbb R\mid |y|<1\}$.
pitfalls: When renaming, replace every occurrence of the bound variable consistently.
A comma between conditions here means AND, not OR.
related: Domain and variable binding (Grundmenge und Variablenbindung)
entries.heading: Auswahl und Ersetzung

entries.short: The union contains elements from at least one of two sets, while the intersection contains only elements from both.
entries.explanation: For sets $A$ and $B$, $A\cup B=\{x\mid x\in A\lor x\in B\}$ and $A\cap B=\{x\mid x\in A\land x\in B\}$. Both set operations form new sets from given sets. The OR in the union is inclusive, so an element may belong to both sets.
pitfalls: The union also contains elements that occur in both sets.
The intersection contains only elements that belong to both sets.
entries.heading: Mengen: Grundidee

entries.short: The unrestricted expression $R=\{x\mid x\notin x\}$ leads to a contradiction when asking whether $R\in R$ holds.
entries.explanation:
The naive rule of forming a set of all objects satisfying any given property would allow $R=\{x\mid x
otin x\}$. If $R\in R$ holds, the condition requires $R
otin R$; if $R
otin R$ holds, $R$ satisfies the condition and must therefore belong to $R$. Both possibilities lead to a contradiction. Axiomatic set theory restricts set formation, for example by using separation to select elements from a set that is already fixed.
entries.example: The barber paradox poses a similar question about self-reference: Does a barber who shaves exactly those men who do not shave themselves shave himself?
pitfalls: The problem arises from unrestricted set formation and the self-referential question, not from every ordinary finite set.
The paradox shows a limit of naive set formation, not an ordinary contradiction in axiomatic set theory.
entries.heading: Russellsche Antinomie
